item.title: When Your Neighbor Has a Weapon for Dogs That You Can't Hear
item.description:
Animal Behavior

When Your Neighbor Has a Weapon for Dogs That You Can't Hear

Remote-controlled devices let anyone punish a dog they don't own, unnoticed.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Some devices reach 300 feet, letting anyone aim ultrasonic pulses at a dog that isn't theirs.
  • A manual trigger lets a neighbor punish a dog at will, whether or not she's even barking.
  • Owners have no way to connect a dog's new anxiety to a stranger's remote control.
  • Anxious, disabled, and very young or old dogs are least equipped to withstand this.

In my last post, I made the case against using ultrasonic bark deterrents on your own dog. This post focuses on another facet of ultrasonic device use—one that is even more insidious, and for which the devices are perfectly designed: silencing a dog that isn't yours, without that dog's owner ever knowing it happened.

Start with the design itself. A remote bark deterrent doesn't require you to own, train, or even like the dog it's punishing. It just needs to be within range. The Dog Silencer MAX, one of the more sensitive units on the market, claims to detect barking from 75 feet and to project its ultrasonic pulse up to 300 feet with a clear line of sight. That's not a device built to correct a dog in your living room. That's a device built to reach across a yard, over a fence, and into a house you've never been inside.

Then there's the handheld remote. Most of these units also ship with a manual trigger — a button you press whenever you hear a bark, sending the pulse regardless of whether the device's own microphone detected anything. In principle, this exists so that an owner farther than 75 feet from the unit can still correct their own dog. In practice, it hands anyone holding the remote the ability to deliver a punishing sound to a dog at will — whether or not that dog is barking, whether or not it's even the dog making noise, whether or not anyone in that house has any idea the device exists. A frustrated neighbor doesn't need to trespass, confront anyone, or leave any evidence. They need a $50 box and a line of sight.

I called this the most insidious feature of the technology when I reviewed it for a legal case, and I'll stand by that description here. It turns a "training tool" into something closer to a weapon that leaves no mark and requires no accountability, because the dog's owner has no way to know the correction is happening, no way to connect their dog's sudden distress to a cause, and often no reason to suspect a neighbor at all. A dog who starts panting, pacing, hiding, or barking more (agitation, not obedience, is a common response to unpredictable aversive stimuli) looks to her owner like a dog with a new behavioral problem. She isn't. She's a dog being punished by a stranger for reasons she can't identify, on a schedule she can't predict, for behavior she may not even be engaging in.

This is where the false-positive problem from Part 1 becomes something worse than an annoyance. These microphones already struggle to distinguish a bark from wind, traffic, or another animal. Add a second household's remote control into the mix, and a dog can be "corrected" for simply existing — for being in her own yard, for another dog barking two houses down, for nothing at all — with zero recourse and zero way for her owner to even diagnose what's happening.

The dogs most likely to be hurt by this aren't the confident, easygoing ones. Dogs with a history of anxiety or trauma tend toward hypervigilance, and are more likely to respond to an unpredictable aversive stimulus with a stronger, more lasting fear response. Dogs with physical disabilities or chronic pain are frequently more sensitive to fearful stimuli in general, and less equipped to recover from repeated stress activation. Puppies under a year have ears that aren't fully developed; senior dogs with hearing loss are, per the manufacturers' own warnings, not supposed to be exposed to these devices at all. None of these dogs consented to being in range of someone else's remote. None of their owners had any say in the matter.

And because these products face essentially no safety regulation and no oversight of how they're marketed or used, there is nothing stopping a neighbor from buying one for exactly this purpose. Nothing on the box says "not for use on dogs you don't own." Nothing requires proof of a barking complaint, a warning, or consent. The device doesn't know or care whose yard it's aimed at.

I don't think most owners of these devices bought them planning to weaponize them against a neighbor's dog. I think most people who buy them are trying to solve a real, exhausting problem — a dog that barks and barks, at 6 a.m., through a shared wall. I have sympathy for that frustration; barking dogs are genuinely hard to live with, and I don't dismiss that. But the same design that makes these devices appealing to a frustrated neighbor — remote, indiscriminate, untraceable — is the design that makes them dangerous in exactly that neighbor's hands. A tool doesn't need malicious intent behind every use to do real harm; it only needs to be available, unregulated, and pointed at a dog who can't opt out and an owner who'll never know why their dog is suddenly afraid.

If you're dealing with a neighbor's barking dog, there are better paths — talking to the owner directly, involving animal control or mediation services, or leaning on the noise ordinances your community already has — that don't involve inflicting an unstudied, high-intensity stimulus on an animal who has no way to understand what's happening to her, or why. And if you're a dog owner whose dog has started acting strangely for no reason you can find, it may be worth asking whether the reason is sitting in a neighbor's drawer.

item.title: The Science of Feeling Worthy
item.description:
Memory

The Science of Feeling Worthy

A novel way to use our memories to actually improve our self-esteem.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Achieving societal milestones often doesn't increase self-worth due to the "arrival fallacy."
  • Our self-esteem is shaped more by memories than by present achievements or status.
  • Memories can be changed each time we recall them, helping reshape self-esteem.

Societal scripts try to convince us that if we achieve [fill in the blank], we’ll finally feel worthy: If we get married, or promoted, or lose weight. Yet, those who achieve these societal trophies often only feel worse. There’s even a scientific term for this dynamic: the arrival fallacy. Dr. Ben Shaar, who created the term, described how people feel when they achieve big goals, “This time, they’re unhappy, but more than that they’re unhappy without hope. Because before they lived under the illusion—well, the false hope—that once they make it, then they’ll be happy.”

Yet, if doing exactly what society tells us won’t make us feel whole, then what will?

The key is that we must stop trying to change our present and start trying to change the past. This is because memory, according to researchers, is a “database for self-esteem.” In Freud’s words, we “suffer mainly from reminiscences.” We feel unworthy—not because we’re not a CEO or supermodel—but because we have memories of rejection, bullying, abuse, or neglect that shape how we see ourselves now.

How Memory Influences Self-Esteem

Change the past? Without functional time machines, it sounds like we’re doomed. And yet, memories have a quirk that offers us hope. Memories are meant to, according to researchers, predict the future rather than record the past. This means they have a mechanism to help them better predict the future: they can be updated each time we remember them.

A novel way to improve self-esteem is to return to a negative memory and picture it having a more positive outcome. To do so, think of a negative memory, one that still troubles you, as vividly as you can. Think about what you saw, felt, smelled, touched, and saw. Describe what this memory means about you as a person and about the world. Then, picture your adult self intervening in the memory in a way that makes the outcome of it more positive.

Examples of Transforming Foundational Memories

You can go back to that breakup and tell yourself how loved you are. You can intervene with that parent screaming at you and tell them to stop, and remind your younger self that you’re safe. You can recall that time you missed the goal and your team lost the game and tell yourself how proud you are of yourself for trying your best, and that your life will soon become much bigger than soccer. In a study where people underwent this memory change procedure, afterward they not only reported feeling better and having less anxiety. They also reported higher self-esteem.

Another study that applied memory reconsolidation found changes in the hippocampus—the part of the brain that records memory—after people revisited the memory and made new meaning.

When we have a foundational memory that makes us feel unworthy—it becomes the lens through which we see everything. We’re less trusting, bracing for the next rejection, scared to ask for our needs, terrified of getting too close again. If someone loves us, they become the exception to the rule of our unworthiness—I’m unworthy and people will reject me aside from this unique instance—but the rule never changes. But what if the foundational memory was the exception rather than the rule? Reconsolidating our memories can reveal that the negative memory—that time you were humiliated by a parent, left alone for too long, or rejected by a former lover—is not the anchor we need to filter everything through but an anomaly that we can finally put to rest.

For science-backed exercises to improve your sense of self-worth, you can read my new book Worth: The New Science of Self-Esteem and Secure Attachment, which is officially out now.

item.title: Who Do You Want to Be in Your Next Chapter?
item.description:
Identity

Who Do You Want to Be in Your Next Chapter?

How to choose what’s next in your life based on who you are.

Posted September 20, 2026

Key points
  • Career and life transitions are opportunities to consider who you are today and who you want to become.
  • We often define ourselves by our skills and knowledge but can’t name our internal strengths and values.
  • Even people who appear strong on the outside often question if they will succeed in new jobs and roles.
Source: wavebreakmedia/Depositphotos

After 16 years climbing corporate ladders, I took the leap to start my business. At the end of a long day arranging my home office, I collapsed on the couch. Looking around, I saw the perfectly beautiful home I owned. I had plaques and pictures on the walls from around the world demonstrating the success I had achieved.

I didn’t feel proud; I just felt numb.

As the sun went down and the room went dark, none of my trophies were visible. Then the words came out of my mouth, “Who are you?” I sat paralyzed for the longest time. I had no answer to the question.

So I decided to go on a vision quest. I bought a big camper trailer and convinced my best friend to spend a month with me exploring some of the beautiful national parks in the West.

We had a wonderful adventure until the last day. I was hiking in a canyon by myself. On the way back, I realized I wasn’t sure I was on the right path. As my heart began to race, my feet sped up to match it. While frantically looking for a familiar ledge or tree, I tripped and fell face down.

I rolled over, looked at the sky, and said, “Got the message. I’m not going to find who I am out here.” I picked myself up and, gratefully, found my way back to my camper.

After returning home and securing enough work to live on, I decided getting another degree might help me find myself. The classes were interesting but it was doing the research for my doctoral dissertation on the challenges smart, strong women face in the workplace that shined the light on my identity problem.

Next-Chapter Criteria

When changing jobs or designing new life chapters, most of the 100 women in my study based their choices on either 1) what they didn’t want to experience anymore or 2) what seemed to fulfill a gnawing sense that there was something more to do. They didn’t have a clear picture of what they wanted to create. What’s worse, they never talked about who they wanted to be.1

Their stories were similar—they wandered from job to job, or from role to role, seeking the one accomplishment that would finally affirm, “You are enough.” They never felt content. No matter how great an achievement, it was never enough.

When I asked them questions about who they were aside from what they could do, like me, they struggled answering the question. Of course, many men are also afflicted with defining themselves by their accomplishments instead of who they are.

A key pattern emerged: the women were strong on the outside, but unsure on the inside. They could identify their performance strengths. They knew what skills and knowledge they had acquired, and what they could quickly learn.

They had developed a strong sense of “what I can do” and a flimsy interpretation of “who I am and can be.” They couldn’t imagine being someone different in a new job or role.

In my book, Wander Woman, I included an exercise to help readers claim their inner powers. To this day, I receive messages from women around the world telling me how the exercise gave them the courage to design their lives based on supporting who they are becoming from the inside out, not just what they can do.

Exercise: Define Yourself by Your Internal Strengths

Step #1: Recall a peak experience where you felt fully alive and fulfilled, a time where you overcame a major challenge in your life or at the completion of an important project or goal. Think back to a moment when you were proud of what you achieved, what you endured, or what you did to lift others up. This moment could have occurred recently or many years ago.

Step #2: List five to 10 character traits you possess that you called on to create this peak experience. Consider your:

  • Internal strengths and gifts.
  • Positive emotions and attitude.
  • Personal values.
  • Unique sense/perspective.

The following list contains examples of traits you might claim. They represent the strengths that make you great even more than your accomplishments.

• Courage • Conviction • Calmness under pressure • Love of life
• Love for people • Confidence • Sense of humor • Playfulness
• Flexibility • Decisiveness • Determination • Integrity • Grace
• Global perspective • Generosity • Loyalty • Honesty • Daring
• Enthusiasm • Gratefulness • Faith • Joyfulness • Trusting
• Peacefulness • Patience • Curiosity • Open mindedness
• Willingness to learn • Creativity • Empathy • Compassion
• Positive energy • Appreciation of differences • Respect
• Responsibility • Commitment • Optimism • Kindness

The list is not complete; include your own words to describe what helps you succeed in life.

The items on your list add up to your ability to confidently step into exciting and fulfilling new chapters and challenges.

Step #3: I AM… Find someone or a group of friends to declare out loud, “I AM…" and state one of your powers. Repeat, “I AM…" with another power until you have declared your entire list. Then every morning, start your day with declaring each of your powers until you embody them as who you are.

Claiming your internal strengths calls on you to release both your fears of how others will judge you and your tendency to judge yourself. When you are asked about your talents and gifts, you won’t be embarrassed to share them. When you face a challenging situation, you can recall your strengths even when you are afraid of failing.

Best of all, you can lose a job, relationship, friends, and wealth, but no one can take away who you are without your permission. You can use your personal powers to keep moving forward, knowing who you will be in your next chapter.

The late activist Audre Lorde said, "When I dare to be powerful—to use my strength in the service of my vision—then it becomes less and less important whether I am afraid.” 2

Whatever you choose as your next job, role, or chapter, be sure you will be honoring who you are from the inside out, not just what you can do.

item.title: When Validation Becomes Expected
item.description:
Social Media

When Validation Becomes Expected

Are social media interactions creating a culture of real-world entitlement?

Posted September 20, 2026

Social media can provide instant access to large audiences and selected communities. It has helped some to stay connected during times of societal challenge, such as the pandemic and other disasters. However, research also shows a less-discussed consequence of social media use: the potential development of entitlement by users that extends into their everyday lives. Although social media use does not automatically make people entitled, some of its core features may encourage expectations of recognition, attention, and reward that are difficult, if not impossible, to sustain in the offline world. This causes a mismatch between what is expected and reality, producing problematic behaviours from those who have been led to believe that the world will respond positively to them.

A characteristic of social media is its reliance on instant or very quick feedback in the form of likes, shares, comments, views, follower counts, etc. Such responses provide users with immediate and measurable forms of social reach—instant gratification. A constant stream of this feedback creates powerful social rewards1 that, for some, can even exert a stronger neural reaction than monetary rewards2. The impact of such digital social rewards may be stronger for those with personality disorders that create a need for social approval, like narcissists. For example, research conducted on undergraduate students3 found that receiving social media likes differentially reduced emotional distress among participants with higher narcissistic traits3. This finding suggests that online validation can become an important source of emotional reinforcement, at least for some with personality deficits.

The Frustration Gap Caused by Social Media

Over time, such feedback can shape people’s expectations, and they may become accustomed to regular praise or engagement online. They may begin to expect similar levels of recognition in workplaces, educational settings, or personal relationships. The result can be frustration when the everyday interactions fail to live up to the unreal world of digital feedback. In a digital environment, where quite ordinary activities can receive public validation, people may gradually start to believe that their opinions, achievements, and experiences deserve constant attention. When this expectation is violated, when expected rewards do not occur, frustration can turn quickly into entitled anger or rage (as displayed by many narcissists). This can affect many, of course, and even the usually placid pigeon, when pushed by unexpected non-reward, can turn aggressive and vent that aggression on its peers4.

Remember, also, that much social media content is curated, so that only the good stuff is posted. Users are exposed to carefully edited versions of other people's lives, often without seeing the hard work, setbacks, or sacrifices behind those achievements. Thus, social media rarely reflects real life, as most users share highlights, rather than hardships or hassles; accomplishments, rather than failures; and celebrations, rather than struggles5. This edited-life material is more likely to get a positive response6, which can amplify the likelihood of frustration-driven entitled outbursts when these unreasonable expectations are violated.

Exposure to this idealised social media content can increase upward social comparison, where individuals compare themselves to people who they perceive as more successful, attractive, accomplished, or popular. Studies have linked these comparisons to lower self-esteem and poorer psychological well-being7,8. Constant exposure to seemingly perfect lives may influence expectations, and, instead of viewing success as something earned through effort and persistence, some may begin to see certain lifestyles or achievements as things they should already have, which can contribute to entitled behaviours when reality does not match online expectations9.

The Illusion of Effortless Success

Influencer culture can amplify these dynamics even further. Millions of users watch content creators receive sponsorships, free products, brand deals, and widespread recognition. Successful influencers invest significant time, creativity, and business expertise into building their audiences. This visibility can create unrealistic assumptions about status and success among their followers. For some individuals, repeated exposure to people being rewarded for sharing content may blur distinctions between popularity and achievement. Recognition becomes something that appears readily available, rather than something earned through expertise, experience, or contribution. Research has highlighted how social media platforms encourage self-promotion and reward attention-seeking behaviour through engagement-driven algorithms10. In such environments, visibility itself can start to feel like a marker of personal value.

Another factor is the highly personalised nature of modern social media platforms. Algorithms are designed to show users content aligned with their interests, preferences, beliefs, and behaviours. As a result, many people spend hours each day in digital environments tailored specifically to them—that is the point of that particular piece of technological engineering. The content they see, the advertisements they receive, and the creators they follow are all selected to hit their interests, and maximise their engagement. However, this reduces exposure to differing viewpoints, and may increase expectations that personal preferences should always be prioritised10. Of course, the offline world operates differently. Relationships of any type, personal or professional, require compromise and cooperation with people who think differently. When individuals become accustomed to digital spaces that revolve almost exclusively around their own interests, they may find these realities more challenging to navigate. This disconnect can foster frustration when real-world interactions fail to conform to personal expectations.

Cultivating Realistic Expectations

Developing awareness of social media's psychological influences is the first step towards counteracting these impacts. Some may say it is the first step in cultivating a healthier engagement but, given the make-up of the forces driving the psychology of the user, it is far from clear that positive outcomes should ever be predicted. Recognising that online content is curated, understanding the limitations of likes and follower counts, and valuing effort over visibility may help people maintain more realistic expectations. By approaching digital interactions more critically and mindfully, people may enjoy whatever benefits of the online communities that they receive, without allowing them to distort their expectations of the real world. In an age when validation is always just a click away, cultivating gratitude, resilience, and perspective may be more important than ever.
